q: A shelter veterinarian in Texas sees a dog with clinical signs highly suspicious for a foreign animal disease (foot-and-mouth disease). There are no laboratory results yet. What is the correct reporting action?
o: Wait for laboratory confirmation, because a clinical diagnosis alone is not sufficient to report.
Report to the local animal control authority and quarantine the animal until laboratory results return.
Contact the state veterinarian and USDA APHIS Veterinary Services immediately, because clinical suspicion alone is enough to report a foreign animal disease.
e: Foreign animal diseases are reported on clinical suspicion, without waiting for confirmation.

q: A disease is reportable in California but not in Colorado. Which statement about the US disease reporting system does this illustrate?
o: Each state keeps its own list of reportable diseases, which vary; the CDC maintains the national list for human diseases (NNDSS) from state reports.
The CDC can override state decisions for nationally notifiable diseases.
The USDA National List of Reportable Animal Diseases is the sole arbiter of what must be reported.
e: State law governs what is reportable within a state, and national systems compile state reports.

q: Which statement about Brucella canis infection in shelter dogs is most accurate?
o: Prolonged combination antibiotic therapy reliably cures it.
It cannot be reliably eliminated with antibiotics, so positive dogs are not considered cured and remain a public health risk.
Serology is not useful, and only blood culture can detect it.
e: Relapses are common after treatment, so dogs positive for B. canis are not considered cured.

q: A shelter in central California receives an outdoor colony cat with fever, marked cervical lymphadenopathy and septic shock. A staff member was scratched without gloves, and the county has documented ground squirrel die-offs. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Suspect plague (Yersinia pestis): isolate the cat with full PPE including an N95, notify the state veterinarian without waiting for laboratory results, and refer the staff member for urgent public health or occupational health evaluation.
Suspect cat scratch disease (Bartonella henselae): routine wound care only for the staff member.
Suspect tularaemia: observe the staff member for 10 days before considering treatment.
e: Cats can transmit pneumonic plague by respiratory droplets, and ground squirrel die-offs are an epizootic warning sign.

q: Following a leptospirosis case, a kennel run is contaminated with urine. Which statement about environmental control of Leptospira is correct?
o: Accelerated hydrogen peroxide is the only effective disinfectant.
Leptospires resist common disinfectants, so the kennel must be taken out of use.
Leptospires are susceptible to common disinfectants and to drying, so standard cleaning and disinfection is effective.
e: Unlike parvovirus, Leptospira does not need specialised products.

q: In which situation does Q fever (Coxiella burnetii) pose the greatest risk to shelter staff?
o: Cleaning kennels occupied by dogs with respiratory disease
Processing blood samples from dogs with tick exposure
Assisting a queen giving birth without respiratory PPE
e: Coxiella burnetii is shed in very high concentrations in birth fluids and placenta, and aerosol inhalation is the main route.

q: Canine influenza H3N2 was first detected in the US in 2015. Which statement best describes the epidemiological significance?
o: It was a re-emergence of an H3N2 strain that had circulated in US dogs in the 1990s.
It was a novel introduction from avian-origin influenza that had adapted to dogs in Asia, so US dogs had no immunity and it spread rapidly through shelters.
It is the same strain as H3N8, which adapted from horses to dogs.
e: A novel virus meets a population with no immunity, so spread through dense dog populations is rapid.

q: Which statement best describes SARS-CoV-2 infection in companion animals from a One Health perspective?
o: It originated in dogs and spilled over to humans.
Cats and dogs are the main reservoir and should be tested routinely in shelters.
It is a human-origin pathogen that has spilled back (reverse zoonosis) into cats, dogs, mink and wildlife.
e: Companion animals are generally infected by their owners, and are not the reservoir.

q: Which methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus is the dominant cause of resistant infections in shelter dogs and cats?
o: Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA)
Staphylococcus pseudintermedius (MRSP)
Staphylococcus schleiferi (MRSS)
e: MRSP is the dominant methicillin-resistant staphylococcus in dogs and a common one in cats.

q: In an outbreak investigation, what is the purpose of a case definition?
o: It states how many animals are required for an outbreak under state law.
It sets the minimum clinical, epidemiological or laboratory criteria that an animal must meet to be counted as a case.
It sets out which animals the shelter is responsible for under its operating agreement.
e: A case definition applies the same criteria across animals so that cases can be counted and compared.

q: An epidemic curve for a shelter parvovirus outbreak shows a sharp, narrow single peak with all cases within 2 days. What type of outbreak does this suggest?
o: Point source, with all animals exposed to the same source at about the same time
Propagated, with cases spreading over successive generations
Continuous common source, with an ongoing contamination source over an extended period
e: A narrow single peak within one incubation period is the classic point-source pattern.

q: During a shelter respiratory disease outbreak, which flow-management practice is most important to limit spread?
o: Staff work with the sick animals first, to finish the highest-risk work early.
Sick and healthy animals are mixed to speed herd immunity.
Staff work with the healthy population first and then the sick or quarantine population, never reversing during a shift.
e: Movement from clean to dirty prevents staff from carrying pathogens to susceptible animals.

q: A shelter is considering emergency vaccination of uninfected dogs during a parvovirus outbreak. What is the rationale and the limitation?
o: It protects all vaccinated dogs immediately, including those already incubating the virus.
It is contraindicated during an outbreak, because modified-live vaccine virus will spread.
It reduces spread to susceptible animals that are not yet exposed, but does not protect dogs that are already incubating infection.
e: Vaccination cannot reverse an infection already under way, and isolation and quarantine are still needed.

q: A state animal health official contacts every shelter in the state each week during respiratory disease season to collect case counts. Which surveillance type is this?
o: Active surveillance
Passive surveillance
Syndromic surveillance
e: Active surveillance means authorities seek out data, rather than waiting for reports.

q: What does the iceberg phenomenon mean in disease surveillance?
o: Laboratory confirmation is needed before cases appear, which hides clinically diagnosed cases.
Passive surveillance captures only the visible tip of the disease burden, and most cases are subclinical, mild or undiagnosed.
Surveillance captures only newly emerged diseases and misses endemic ones.
e: Most cases never reach surveillance systems, so passive data underestimate burden.

q: What does biobanking mean in shelter disease surveillance?
o: Maintaining a database of adoption records linked to veterinary outcomes
Storing vaccines at temperatures that keep them potent
Preserving diagnostic samples (serum, tissue, faeces) from unexplained deaths and disease clusters for retrospective testing if a new pathogen is later identified
e: Stored samples let new tests be applied to past events.

q: A shelter joins a regional collaborative that shares de-identified aggregate disease data weekly across 12 shelters. What is the main surveillance benefit?
o: Regional outbreaks that no single shelter would detect alone become visible when cases are aggregated.
It replaces passive reporting to state and federal agencies.
It lets the state veterinarian audit individual animal records.
e: Pooling data across facilities increases the power to detect clusters.

q: From a One Health perspective, which best describes the shelter veterinarian's role in disease surveillance?
o: Clinician only, with surveillance left to public health officials
Reporter of zoonotic diseases only, with animal-only diseases not requiring reporting
Clinician, infection-control officer, mandatory reporter and surveillance node, integrating animal health, public health and the community
e: Shelter veterinarians are often the first to detect disease in the community animal population.

q: Which agent did viral metagenomics implicate as most likely responsible for the shelter vomiting outbreak?
o: Rotavirus I
Feline astrovirus
Carnivore bocaparvovirus 3
Norovirus GVI
e: Feline astrovirus was present in all pools at high prevalence and temporally tied to the outbreak.

q: What did testing of asymptomatic control cats housed in the same areas reveal?
o: About 56% were also shedding astrovirus
None were shedding the virus
They cleared infection in 24 hours
All were shedding rotavirus
e: 5 of 9 (56%) clinically unaffected control cats also shed astrovirus, indicating significant asymptomatic shedding.

q: Fecal samples collected ~1 year before and after the outbreak supported which conclusion?
o: The outbreak was caused by panleukopenia
Shedding lasted under 24 hours
Astrovirus is a normal commensal in this shelter
Astrovirus was only temporarily associated with the outbreak
e: No astrovirus was detected before or after, so the virus was temporarily linked to the outbreak rather than commensal.

q: Which species, unlike rabbits, was highly susceptible to SARS-CoV-2 AND transmitted it between conspecifics?
o: Rabbits (Oryctolagus cuniculus)
Raccoon dogs
Egyptian rousettes
White-tailed deer
e: Raccoon dogs were highly susceptible and could transmit between conspecifics, unlike rabbits which did not transmit.

q: What key shortcoming did the authors highlight regarding SARS-CoV-2 in animals?
o: No human cases to compare
Absence of an adequate animal surveillance system to follow viral evolution
Lack of any susceptible species
Overuse of animal vaccines
e: They stress that animal circulation has not been matched by an adequate surveillance system to track viral evolution.

q: Which wild animals were described as potential natural reservoirs of SARS-CoV-2?
o: White-tailed deer, Egyptian rousettes, and minks
Horses and cattle
Salmon and trout
Pigeons and rats
e: White-tailed deer, Egyptian rousettes, and minks were named as potential natural reservoirs.

q: During the 2020–22 highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) H5 epidemics monitored in the Netherlands, HPAI H5 infection was reported in how many wild bird species?
e: Infection was reported across 51 bird species during the two epidemic seasons.

q: During the 2020–22 highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) H5 epidemics in the Netherlands, which statement best describes the wild bird species groups with the highest reported mortality?
o: Varied per epidemic year (geese versus sea birds)
Were only raptors
Included no waterfowl
Were identical each year
e: 2020–21 mainly affected Anatidae/barnacle geese; 2021–22 hit sea birds (Sandwich terns and northern gannets).

q: The recommended surveillance approach was to:
o: Monitor live and dead wild birds
Cull all poultry
Stop monitoring wild birds
Vaccinate wild birds
e: Monitoring live and dead wild birds was recommended for tracking HPAI dynamics.

q: The most plausible source of H5N1 infection in mammals was:
o: Contaminated water only
Close contact with or ingestion of infected birds
Mosquito bites
Human handlers
e: Close contact with and ingestion of infected birds was the most plausible source.

q: Compared with previous waves, the current panzootic affected:
o: Only poultry
A larger geographic area and more mammal species
Fewer species and a smaller area
No mammals
e: >48 species across 26 countries, a far larger scope than prior waves.

q: The review warns that H5N1 may be:
o: Adapting to infect mammals, raising pandemic concern
Already eradicated
Permanently limited to birds
Becoming less infectious
e: Mutations and possible mammal-to-mammal transmission suggest adaptation and pandemic risk.

q: How was highly pathogenic avian influenza (H5N1) confirmed in this cat's brain and lung tissue?
o: Blood culture
Serology
Indirect fluorescent antibody
Real-time RT-PCR
e: Influenza A/H5 was confirmed in brain and pulmonary tissues by real-time RT-PCR.

q: A case report documented multisystemic H5N1 highly pathogenic avian influenza in a 4.5-year-old male castrated domestic shorthair cat, confirmed by real-time RT-PCR in both lung and brain tissues. What exposure feature did this case highlight as novel?
o: Extensive outdoor roaming
A predominantly indoor cat with minimal outdoor access
Known contact with an infected cat
Recent vaccination failure
e: Infection occurred in a largely indoor cat with minimal known outdoor access, supporting the possibility of indirect environmental contamination or unrecognized transport hosts and expanding the understood exposure risk for feline H5N1.

q: A 4.5-year-old predominantly indoor domestic shorthair cat presented with lethargy, fever, severe respiratory distress, and neurologic dysfunction confirmed to be H5N1 highly pathogenic avian influenza. Despite aggressive supportive care, what was the outcome?
o: Spontaneous resolution
Full recovery
Humane euthanasia after deterioration
Improvement on antivirals
e: Despite intravenous fluids, antiemetics, and NSAIDs, the cat's condition rapidly deteriorated, necessitating humane euthanasia.
